mcqs.question: A library ships `4.2.0 -> 4.2.1` under semantic versioning. What can a consumer conclude without reading the diff?
options: It's a bug fix release with no intentional behavior change for correct usage — safe to upgrade without code changes
New backward-compatible functionality was added
Something backward-incompatible changed and code may need updates
The major version's public API was completely rewritten
mcqs.explanation: The patch position's entire promise is bug fixes with no intended behavior change for correctly-used code, which is what lets consumers auto-upgrade patches without review. New functionality is a minor bump, and anything breaking or API-rewriting belongs in a major bump — neither describes a patch release.

mcqs.question: A mobile app team ships on a fixed two-week release train instead of releasing each change the moment it's ready. What's the main reason?
options: Continuous release always ships smaller, safer changes than a release train
Fixed-cadence releases are always faster to ship than continuous ones
Release trains produce fewer bugs per release than continuous release
Something external to the code — app store review time and a predictable cadence users and support teams can plan around — makes an unpredictable, whenever-ready release schedule impractical
mcqs.explanation: Release trains exist for external constraints like app store review windows and the need for a predictable cadence that other teams can plan around, not because they're inherently faster or produce fewer bugs — continuous release, when it fits the delivery model, ships smaller batches and often has better bug attribution precisely because each release is small.

mcqs.question: While preparing an urgent hotfix for v2.4.1, an engineer notices an unrelated small improvement and considers including it in the same hotfix branch. What's the risk?
options: There's no risk — bundling small improvements into a hotfix saves a release cycle
The unrelated change is untested against production under time pressure, defeating the entire purpose of keeping a hotfix minimal and de-risked
Hotfix branches can only ever contain exactly one file change
It would make the version number invalid
mcqs.explanation: A hotfix's safety comes from its narrow scope — branching from the released tag and shipping only the fix means the change surface under time pressure is as small as possible. Adding an unrelated improvement reintroduces exactly the untested-change risk a hotfix exists to avoid, regardless of file count or version numbering, which are unaffected either way.

mcqs.question: Why does semver discipline matter more, not less, as a library's dependent count grows?
options: Larger libraries are given a grace period by package registries for mislabeled releases
Dependency resolvers use semver ranges to auto-upgrade patch/minor releases with no human review, so a mislabeled release can silently break thousands of consumers automatically
Larger dependent counts mean fewer people will notice a mislabeled release
Semver only applies to libraries below a certain download threshold
mcqs.explanation: Package managers resolve semver ranges automatically and pull in patch/minor bumps with no human reviewing the change first, so scale amplifies the blast radius of a mislabeled release rather than shrinking it — more dependents means more automatic upgrades happen unattended, not fewer people noticing.

mcqs.question: A one-line change lowering a default timeout from 30s to 5s ships as a patch release. Some consumers relying on the old default start seeing failures. What was misjudged?
options: The change was judged by lines of diff instead of by behavioral impact on consumers — a default change that reasonable consumers depend on is breaking, regardless of diff size
Patch releases are not allowed to touch configuration defaults at all
The bug is really in the consumers' code for depending on a default value
Nothing was misjudged — timeouts are implementation details exempt from semver
mcqs.explanation: Semver classifies changes by their effect on consumers, not by how many lines changed — a small diff that alters a widely-relied-on default is exactly the kind of breaking change semver exists to flag with a major bump. Depending on a documented default is reasonable consumer behavior, not a bug on their end, and defaults are not exempt from the contract.
